chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Ja'far ibn Hanan said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who endowed his produce (gallah) for his relatives from his father and his relatives from his mother, and bequeathed to a man and his descendants from that produce, who had no kinship with him, three hundred dirhams every year, and distributed the remainder among his relatives from his father and from his mother. He (AS) said: 'It is permissible for the one to whom he bequeathed that.'

I said: 'What do you think if the produce of the land he endowed yields only five hundred dirhams?' He said: 'Is it not in his bequest that the one to whom he bequeathed receives three hundred dirhams from the produce, and the remainder is distributed among his relatives from his father and mother?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'His relatives cannot take anything from the produce until the bequequeathed person is paid three hundred dirhams; then they have what remains after that.'

I said: 'What do you think if the one to whom he bequeathed dies?' He said: 'If he dies, the three hundred dirhams belong to his heirs; they inherit it as long as any of them remain. When his heirs are cut off and none of them remain, the three hundred dirhams belong to the relatives of the deceased; it is returned to what comes out of the endowment, then it is distributed among them; they inherit that as long as they remain, and the produce continues.'

I said: 'Do the heirs of the deceased have the right to sell the land if they need it and what comes out of the produce is not sufficient for them?' He said: 'Yes, if they all agree and the sale is better for them, they sell.'
ai.seo_question: What are the rules for distributing produce from an endowed land when a fixed amount is bequeathed to a non-relative?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes the principle of priority in waqf distributions, ensuring that specific bequests to non-relatives are fulfilled before relatives receive their share, even if the yield is limited. It further clarifies the hereditary nature of this fixed bequest, noting that upon the beneficiary's death, the right reverts to the donor's relatives, illustrating the flexibility of private endowments in Shia jurisprudence. The ruling also permits the sale of the endowed land by heirs if it serves their best interest, highlighting the pragmatic approach to managing waqf assets.
